label: ex:hodge-su2
title: Hodge star on $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$
html:
Example. Hodge star on \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))

Continuing higher forms on SU(2), the Hodge star on A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) identifies \Omega^k(A) with \Omega^{n-k}(A) using the Frobenius form. On the 3D-calculus \Omega^{\bullet}(A), the volume form is \mathrm{vol} = \omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3 (normalised by \int_A(\mathrm{vol}) = 1). Then:

  • \star 1 = \mathrm{vol}, \star\mathrm{vol} = 1.
  • On 1-forms: \star\omega_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_{ijk} \omega_j \wedge \omega_k.
  • On 2-forms: \star(\omega_i \wedge \omega_j) = \epsilon_{ijk}\omega_k.

The self-dual 2-forms \Omega^+(A) are the +1-eigenspace of \star. In 3 dimensions, \star maps \Omega^2(A) to \Omega^1(A), so the self-dual decomposition is trivial. The non-trivial decomposition arises when \dim H = 4.
